description: How radio, infrared and space telescopes reveal what optical instruments miss, and what CCDs add to astronomy.
content_html:
Beyond Visible Light

Optical telescopes gather visible light — but the universe radiates across the entire electromagnetic spectrum. Hot gas emits X-rays; cold dust clouds glow in infrared; accelerating electrons in magnetic fields produce radio waves. To build a complete picture of the cosmos, astronomers have built telescopes sensitive to radio waves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Each wavelength window reveals phenomena invisible to all others.

CCD Detectors and Digital Imaging

CCD (charge-coupled device) detectors have replaced photographic film in modern telescopes. CCDs convert incoming photons into electrical charge and store the charge in a grid of pixels. They are far more efficient than film: a typical CCD detects about 90% of incoming photons (quantum efficiency of ~90%), compared with only a few percent for film. The recorded data are image files that can be processed digitally — brightening faint features, subtracting sky background, stacking multiple exposures to reduce noise. CCDs work across a wide wavelength range, from near-ultraviolet to near-infrared.

Why the Atmosphere Limits Telescopes

Earth’s atmosphere absorbs or scatters most of the electromagnetic spectrum. Only two main windows allow radiation to reach ground level:

  • The optical window — visible light and small parts of the near-infrared and near-ultraviolet. This is why conventional ground-based telescopes work.
  • The radio window — radio waves from about 1 mm to 10 m wavelength pass through relatively freely. This allows ground-based radio astronomy.

Ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma-ray and most infrared radiation is absorbed before reaching sea level. Additionally, the atmosphere causes atmospheric seeing — turbulent air cells refract starlight, making stars twinkle and blurring fine detail in optical images. This limits the resolution of ground-based telescopes regardless of their size.

Key Fact

Earth’s atmosphere transmits only the optical window (visible light) and the radio window. All other wavebands (UV, X-ray, gamma ray, most IR) are absorbed by the atmosphere and require telescopes at high altitude or in space.

Radio Telescopes

A simple radio telescope consists of a large parabolic dish that focuses radio waves onto a receiver at the focal point, similar in principle to a reflecting optical telescope. Radio wavelengths (centimetres to metres) are much longer than visible light, which creates two challenges:

  • Resolution — angular resolution depends on wavelength divided by aperture. Longer wavelengths produce poorer (larger) resolution for a given dish size. A single dish must be enormous to achieve decent resolution. Jodrell Bank’s Lovell Telescope (76 m diameter) achieves only modest angular resolution at typical radio wavelengths.
  • Aperture synthesis — instead of a single enormous dish, astronomers link many smaller dishes spread over long baselines using a technique called aperture synthesis. The Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico uses 27 dishes spread over up to 36 km, achieving the resolution equivalent to a single dish 36 km across. This is the principle behind very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), where dishes on different continents are combined.

Radio observations have revealed features invisible in optical wavelengths: the large-scale structure of the Milky Way’s spiral arms (mapped using neutral hydrogen’s 21 cm emission line); jets of particles emitted by active galaxies and quasars; protoplanetary discs of gas and dust around young stars; and the cold molecular clouds where star formation begins. Pulsars — rapidly rotating neutron stars — were first detected at radio wavelengths. The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation peaks at millimetre wavelengths and was first detected with radio receivers.

Infrared Telescopes

Infrared radiation is absorbed mainly by water vapour in the lower atmosphere. To observe at infrared wavelengths, telescopes must be built at high-altitude dry sites — such as Mauna Kea in Hawaii (altitude 4,200 m) or the Atacama Desert in Chile — where the atmosphere above is thin and dry. Even better, space-based infrared telescopes avoid all atmospheric absorption. Infrared astronomy reveals: molecular clouds and protostars hidden behind dust (dust absorbs visible light but is largely transparent in infrared); galaxies that emit most of their energy in infrared (starburst galaxies); and the thermal glow of cool objects such as brown dwarfs and exoplanets.

Space Telescopes

Space telescopes operate above the atmosphere entirely, solving both the absorption problem and the seeing problem. Key examples:

  • Hubble Space Telescope (HST) — optical and near-UV/near-IR. Its position above the atmosphere gives it resolution far exceeding ground-based telescopes of similar size. Images from HST of the Hubble Deep Field showed thousands of galaxies in a tiny patch of sky, demonstrating the depth of the observable universe.
  • James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) — primarily infrared. Its gold-coated beryllium mirror (6.5 m) and cool operating temperature (~40 K, shielded from the Sun) allow it to detect extremely faint infrared signals from the earliest galaxies and from exoplanet atmospheres during transits.

X-rays and gamma rays require space-based detectors. X-ray telescopes (such as the ESA XMM-Newton and NASA Chandra) use grazing-incidence mirrors — X-rays bounce off mirrors only at very shallow angles. X-ray observations reveal hot gas in galaxy clusters, accretion discs around black holes, neutron star binary systems, and the hot corona of the Sun. Gamma-ray observatories (such as NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope) detect gamma-ray bursts — the most energetic explosions in the universe — and jets from active galaxies. Because X-ray and gamma-ray photons are so energetic, they can be detected by sensors sensitive to individual photon impacts rather than traditional mirrors that focus light.

What Telescopes Reveal About Familiar Objects

Even objects visible to the naked eye look dramatically different through a telescope. Double stars (two stars close together in the sky) may be resolved into separate points. Some double stars are true binary stars — gravitationally bound pairs — while others are merely optical doubles (coincidentally aligned along the line of sight). Open clusters reveal dozens of individual stars. Globular clusters appear as a dense ball of stars. Nebulae show as glowing or dark patches of gas and dust. Distant galaxies appear as fuzzy ellipses or spiral forms at the limits of resolution.

Key Fact

Each waveband faces a specific atmospheric problem. Visible and radio sneak through — infrared is blocked by water vapour (high-altitude observatories help), ultraviolet and X-ray are blocked by ozone and nitrogen (space telescopes only), and gamma rays need detectors above the atmosphere because they hit the air and shower into secondary particles.
exam_tip_html: For questions on why certain telescopes must be in space, give two distinct reasons: (1) the atmosphere absorbs the relevant waveband, and (2) the atmosphere causes blurring (seeing) even in the optical window. For radio telescope questions, make sure you explain why large dishes or aperture synthesis arrays are needed — it’s because resolution is proportional to aperture divided by wavelength, and radio wavelengths are very long. When naming space telescopes, Hubble (optical) and JWST (infrared) are the most useful examples; always link the telescope to the waveband it observes and what it reveals that ground-based telescopes cannot.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Earth’s atmosphere has two windows: the optical window (visible light) and the radio window. All other wavebands require high-altitude or space-based telescopes. CCD detectors replaced film, with ~90% quantum efficiency.
  • Radio telescopes use large parabolic dishes; aperture synthesis (e.g. VLA) combines multiple dishes to simulate a larger aperture and achieve better resolution. Infrared telescopes need dry high-altitude sites or space to avoid water-vapour absorption.
  • Space telescopes (HST for optical/UV, JWST for infrared, XMM-Newton/Chandra for X-ray) avoid atmospheric absorption and seeing entirely, revealing galaxies, protostars, exoplanet atmospheres, black holes and gamma-ray bursts.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following wavebands can be observed from the ground at sea level?
A) X-rays
B) Gamma rays
C) Radio waves
D) Extreme ultraviolet
State two advantages of CCDs over photographic film for recording astronomical images.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each (up to 2) for any of:
• Much higher quantum efficiency (detect ~90% of photons vs a few % for film) [1]
• Data stored as digital files that can be processed, stacked and analysed on computers [1]
• Linear response (brightness proportional to detected photons) [1]
• Reusable; no need to replace film after each exposure [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a single radio telescope dish needs to be much larger than an optical telescope to achieve a similar angular resolution.
practice_questions.marks: Angular resolution depends on wavelength divided by aperture diameter [1]. Radio wavelengths (centimetres to metres) are millions of times longer than optical wavelengths (hundreds of nanometres) [1]. Therefore, to achieve the same resolving power as an optical telescope of a given size, a radio dish must be far larger — or multiple dishes must be combined using aperture synthesis to simulate a larger aperture [1].

practice_questions.text: Compare the advantages and limitations of ground-based optical telescopes and space-based telescopes for astronomical observation.
practice_questions.marks:
Ground-based optical:
• Advantage: much cheaper to build and maintain; can be upgraded; large mirrors achievable (e.g. 10 m class telescopes) [1]
• Limitation: atmospheric absorption blocks non-optical wavebands; atmospheric seeing blurs images even in visible light [1]

Space-based:
• Advantage: no atmospheric absorption — can observe all wavebands; no atmospheric seeing — achieves diffraction-limited resolution [1]
• Limitation: expensive to build and launch; cannot be easily repaired (though HST was serviced by shuttle missions); mirror size limited by launch vehicle fairing [1]

Mark up to 4: 1 per correct paired comparison point, max 2 per telescope type.

practice_questions.text:
Megan Cartwright is a student at the Holt Astronomy Group who wants to observe a newly discovered young stellar object (a protostar) hidden inside a dense molecular cloud. She asks whether she should use an optical telescope, a radio telescope or an infrared space telescope.

Evaluate which type of telescope would be most suitable for this observation and explain why the other two options are less effective.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Recommends infrared space telescope (e.g. JWST); explains that the molecular cloud absorbs visible light so the protostar is invisible to optical telescopes (dust is opaque to visible); infrared radiation penetrates dust clouds because infrared wavelengths are longer and less scattered; space-based removes atmospheric water-vapour absorption that blocks mid-infrared from the ground; radio telescopes would detect cold molecular gas surrounding the region but not the thermal emission of the protostar itself; optical telescope would see only the dark cloud silhouette or surrounding stars, not the hidden protostar.

Secure (3-4): Recommends infrared; explains why visible light is blocked by dust; some explanation of why radio and optical are less effective; may omit space vs ground distinction.

Developing (1-2): Recommends a plausible telescope with limited justification.

Emerging (0): Irrelevant or no response.

practice_questions.text: The Very Large Array (VLA) uses 27 dishes spread across a maximum baseline of 36 km. Explain what aperture synthesis is and why this technique is necessary for achieving useful resolution with radio telescopes.
practice_questions.marks: Aperture synthesis links multiple smaller dishes electronically to simulate the resolution of a single dish equal in size to the maximum separation (baseline) between them [1]. This is necessary because single dishes of 36 km diameter are impractical to build [1]. Radio wavelengths are so long that even a 36-km effective aperture achieves only moderate angular resolution compared with optical telescopes [1].

knowledge_checks.q: Which two atmospheric windows allow ground-based astronomy?
What makes CCDs more useful than photographic film in modern telescopes?
options: Much higher quantum efficiency (~90%) and digital data output
They work only in visible light, reducing interference
They can be used without a telescope mount
They eliminate the need for focusing the telescope

knowledge_checks.q: Aperture synthesis combines multiple smaller radio dishes to simulate the resolution of a single dish the size of the _____ between the dishes.
Infrared telescopes at high-altitude sites like Mauna Kea are placed there to reduce absorption by atmospheric _____.
Match each telescope type to what it primarily reveals.
right: Neutral hydrogen distribution and galactic structure
Accretion discs around black holes and hot gas in clusters

flashcard_questions.q: What does CCD stand for, and what does it do?
flashcard_questions.a: Charge-coupled device; it converts photons into electrical signals, recording a digital astronomical image.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do radio telescopes need very large dishes or aperture synthesis arrays?
flashcard_questions.a: Radio wavelengths are very long, so angular resolution is poor unless the effective aperture is enormous.
Linking multiple small dishes electronically to simulate the resolution of a single dish the size of their maximum separation.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two wavebands that cannot be observed from sea level.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: X-rays, gamma rays, most ultraviolet, most infrared.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must infrared telescopes be placed at high altitude or in space?
flashcard_questions.a: Water vapour in the lower atmosphere absorbs infrared radiation.

flashcard_questions.q: What does atmospheric seeing cause in optical observations?
flashcard_questions.a: Atmospheric turbulence refracts starlight, blurring images and making stars appear to twinkle.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main advantage of the Hubble Space Telescope over a ground-based optical telescope of the same size?
flashcard_questions.a: No atmospheric absorption or seeing; achieves diffraction-limited resolution.

flashcard_questions.q: What does JWST primarily observe, and what does its position in space allow it to detect?
flashcard_questions.a: JWST observes infrared; its cold, space-based position lets it detect faint infrared from early galaxies and exoplanet atmospheres.

flashcard_questions.q: What did radio telescopes reveal about the structure of the Milky Way?
flashcard_questions.a: The spiral arm structure, mapped using neutral hydrogen's 21 cm emission line.

flashcard_questions.q: What are X-ray telescopes used to observe?
flashcard_questions.a: Accretion discs around black holes, hot gas in galaxy clusters, and neutron star binaries.
Two stars gravitationally bound to each other, orbiting their common centre of mass.

glossary_terms.definition: Charge-coupled device; a silicon sensor that converts incoming photons to electrical signals, recording a digital astronomical image with high efficiency.
Blurring of astronomical images caused by turbulent air cells in Earth's atmosphere refracting starlight, limiting resolution of ground-based optical telescopes.
A bowl-shaped reflector used in radio telescopes to focus incoming radio waves onto a receiver at the focal point.
A technique combining signals from multiple radio telescope dishes spread over a long baseline to achieve the resolution of a single dish the size of the maximum separation.
A dense, cold cloud of gas and dust in which new stars form; absorbs visible light but emits in infrared and radio.
Two stars gravitationally bound to each other and orbiting their common centre of mass.
The narrow range of wavelengths (roughly visible light) that passes through Earth's atmosphere to reach sea-level telescopes.

items.title: A Flight Through the Universe by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey
items.description: Created using CCD data from the SDSS — a real-world showcase of what digital sky surveys with high quantum-efficiency detectors can reveal about cosmic structure.

items.title: Black Holes: The Edge of All We Know (2021)
items.description: Follows the Event Horizon Telescope team capturing the first black hole image using radio aperture synthesis — directly illustrates the telescope network described in this lesson.

items.title: Contact (1997)
items.description: The VLA radio telescope array features prominently — the film captures how radio astronomy scans billions of star systems for signals from other civilisations.

items.title: ESA: James Webb Space Telescope
items.description: Full technical overview of JWST — its infrared mirrors, L2 positioning, cryogenic cooling and first science results, directly extending the space telescope content in this lesson.
